books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Figures from the Provost Marshal General’s report, as summarized in the 1956 report Veterans in Our Society (U.S. Government Printing Office). Figures are rounded.
stimulus.text:
Results of the four drafts under the Enrollment Act of 1863.

| Outcome | Men |
| Names drawn | 776,829 |
| Men who furnished substitutes | 73,607 |
| Men who paid $300 commutation | 86,724 |
| Men exempted | 315,509 |
| Men who failed to report | 161,244 |
| Men who entered the army as draftees | 46,347 |

Altogether 119,954 men entered the army under the act: 46,347 draftees plus 73,607 hired substitutes. The rows overlap, so they do not add to the total drawn.

stem: The New York City draft riots began as protests at draft offices but turned violent. The rioters’ anger fell hardest on the city’s Black residents, whom they blamed for the war. That turn shows the riots were driven by

options.text: class resentment mixed with racial hatred, not opposition to the war alone.
support for the Confederacy among all New Yorkers alike.
options.misconception: Background: New York City was divided, and many New Yorkers supported the Union; the rioters did not speak for all of the city.

options.text: a demand to end slavery at once, everywhere in the country.
options.misconception: Background: the rioters attacked Black New Yorkers and blamed them for the war; they were not demanding abolition.

options.text: a plot organized in secret by the Confederate government.
options.misconception: Background: the riots grew out of anger at the draft and at Black workers; they were not a Confederate plot.

rationales.B: Background: New York City was divided, and many New Yorkers supported the Union; the rioters did not speak for all of the city.
rationales.C: Background: the rioters attacked Black New Yorkers and blamed them for the war; they were not demanding abolition.
rationales.D: Background: the riots grew out of anger at the draft and at Black workers; they were not a Confederate plot.
rationales.A: The riots began against the draft and its 300 dollar escape fee, then turned on Black New Yorkers, so class anger and racial hatred drove them together.
rationales.general:
1. Start where the riots started: at the draft offices, against the 300 dollar fee.
2. Then watch where the anger moves: onto Black New Yorkers, blamed for taking jobs and for the war.
3. Background: at least 120 people were killed in the riots, many of them Black.
4. Two angers are working at once, and the second one picks the victims.
Remember: when a protest changes targets, the new target tells you what else was driving it.
